Se essa aproximação não permite a manutenção do quadro brandomiano de Between Saying and Doing, o paralelo com Making it Explicit traz uma consequência importante para a compreensão do projeto da Inteligência Artificial Explicável, a saber, tornar explícitos os comprometimentos inferenciais implícitos de processos decisórios que afetam nossa vida em comum.

items.title: The Cohesive Tetrad as an Epistemic-Ethical Framework for Truth Governance: A Conditional Gold Standard under Minimal Human Dignity Axioms.
items.abstract: Contemporary institutions increasingly rely on metrics, models and codified procedures, yet public trust in their truth claims continues to erode. The central problem addressed is how to design an architecture of truth governance that remains normatively robust and publicly accountable under conditions of epistemic pluralism and technological mediation. This article argues that the erosion of trust does not stem only from technical error but from an overly narrow architecture that reduces persons to data, rules or preferences. Using The Cohesive Tetrad as a conceptual lens, the study develops an axiomatic model, proposed as a conditional gold standard for truth governance under minimal human dignity axioms, that treats four “languages of truth” as jointly necessary for responsible judgment: Sabda as the revelatory word and source of norm and telos, Logika as disciplined reasoning, Qualia as lived experience, and Mistika as the intensional spiritual calibration of intention, with Akhlak as the observable surface where their convergence is tested. Methodologically the article adopts a normative conceptual design: it formulates minimal epistemic axioms centred on human dignity, integrity, coherence, non-reduction and self-correction, defines the internal relations of the Tetrad under these axioms, and compares the resulting architecture with data-centred, rule-centred and virtue-centred approaches in philosophy of science and public ethics. The analysis shows that monolinguistic regimes of truth tend to generate specific structural failure modes, whereas the Tetrad yields a non-reductive matrix that can host multiple methodologies while keeping Akhlak as verification. The article concludes that, under the stated axioms, The Cohesive Tetrad offers a coherent and practically relevant framework for truth governance in law, policy and AI, while remaining open to empirical testing and intercultural refinement.

items.title: Rethinking Psychiatric Experience Life Narratives, Ontological Insecurity, and Collaborative Knowledge Production in Mental Health Research.
items.abstract: This article examines how psychiatric experiences shape life narratives while proposing innovative methodological approaches for mental health research. Drawing on four case studies of individuals diagnosed with bipolar disorder, the research initially reveals how psychiatric service users’ life stories often become “pathographies”—narratives predominantly organized around illness and medical interventions. However, through a shift to collaborative research methods, participants moved beyond these initial illness-centered accounts to develop more complex understandings of their experiences. The analysis employs R.D. Laing’s concept of ontological insecurity and Michel Foucault’s framework of historical ontology to examine how psychiatric interventions affect individuals’ sense of reality, identity, and time. The findings demonstrate how collaborative dialogue can transform ontologically insecure experiences into shared grounds for generating new meanings and critical insights about psychiatric systems. This approach addresses key methodological challenges in mental health research while contributing to debates about experiential knowledge and the democratization of mental health knowledge production. The study suggests that, although biographical narratives provide valuable research foundations, their greatest potential lies in creating opportunities for collaborative examination and critique that empower individuals to develop more restorative and emancipatory understandings of their experiences.

items.title: Tractatus epistemo-logicus, oder ‚Was ist Erkenntnis?‘ – Eine Fundamentalkritik der philosophischen Erkenntnistheorie und ihrer Heuristik – und ein Gegenentwurf.
items.abstract: Die Gleichsetzung von Wissen mit Gewissheit im Sinne von Kants Frage „Was können wir wissen?“ ist grundlegend für die Heuristik der philosophischen Erkenntnistheorie. Die Frage der Gewissheit unseres Wissens als Kernfrage der Erkenntnistheorie setzt ihrerseits eine Idee davon, was Wissen und Erkenntnis ist, als ihren notwendigen Referenzpunkt voraus. Grundlegend für die Idee von Wissen und Erkenntnis im allgemeinen ist die formale Unterscheidung zwischen Inhalt und Gegenstand der Erkenntnis. Konstitutiv für die philosophische Erkenntnistheorie ist darüber hinaus die Konzeption von Erkenntnis als lineare Subjekt-Objekt-Beziehung, und zwar im Sinne einer unvermittelten Gegenüberstellung von Subjekt und Objekt. Diese impliziert, dass der empirische Inhalt der Erkenntnis nicht anders, als mit direktem Bezug auf das Objekt der Erkenntnis definierbar ist, also im Wege des heuristischen Kurzschlusses des Inhalts mit dem Gegenstand der Erkenntnis. Als einziges Element der Vermittlung des empirischen Inhalts kommt in diesem Setting das Konzept der passiven Rezeption, in Gestalt der unmittelbaren Sinneseindrücke, in Frage, das wiederum bedingt, dass die einzige Frage, die sich bezüglich des empirischen Inhalts der Erkenntnis überhaupt stellen lässt, eben die Frage der Gewissheit ist, und zwar vorwiegend betreffend den Anspruch von Aussagen auf Allgemeingültigkeit. Ganz andere, grundlegendere Fragen stellen sich, wenn man – wiederum mit Bezug auf die Unterscheidung zwischen Inhalt und Gegenstand – Erkenntnis unbefangen als ein Phänomen betrachtet; und zwar vor allem die Frage der Provenienz (Genese, Generierung) des Inhalts der Erkenntnis, losgelöst von der (ontologisch präformierten) Frage der Gewissheit. Nicht zuletzt deshalb, weil auch das erkennende Subjekt selbst offensichtlich (und zwar nicht nur im Rahmen der Erkenntnistheorie) ein Objekt der Erkenntnis ist, und insofern eben als Bezugspunkt der Erkenntnistheorie (aus Erkenntnissicht) selbst einen Erkenntnisinhalt bildet (was die Idee der Gewissheit als subjektives Kriterium grundlegend entwertet). Womit sich die Frage nach dem geeigneten Rahmen dieser Selbstbestimmung des erkennenden Subjekts stellt; mit direkten Auswirkungen auf die Grundkonzeption des Phänomens Erkenntnis und, wie sich zeigen wird, weitreichenden Folgen für die Antwort auf die Frage ‚Was ist Erkenntnis?‘.

items.title: The Promise of Contract Pluralism.
items.abstract: Many contract theorists argue that contracts are promises. This view is appealing because it can justify the institution of contract law—contract law allows parties to vindicate their promissory rights. But contract-as-promise advocates have seriously misunderstood how promises work. They assume a cartoon version of promises, one that is overly abstract, individualistic, and is singularly fixated on the obligation to do what one promised. Such theorists have failed to adequately attend to other important dimensions of promises: How stringent is the promise? Under what conditions is a person obligated to perform? How is an agent entitled to respond to a breach? How should a promisee respond to a request for release? When should a promisee agree to renegotiate? These features of promissory morality vary radically across different kinds of human relationships—e.g., marriage, friendship, employment, parenting, and commercial bargains. This is an important result for contract theory. Courts routinely invoke the idea of a general, uniform set of contract principles applicable to all contracts. But if promissory morality doesn’t justify applying uniform contract principles across different contracting relationships, then likely nothing does. We should thus liberate ourselves from the idea of general contract principles and embrace a kind of contractual pluralism.

items.title: Critical, Creative, and Caring Thinking.
items.abstract: Este breve artículo presenta la opinión de que la teoría Lipman/Sharp del pensamiento crítico, creativo y solidario está prosperando, habiendo sido adaptada y desarrollada aún más en el contexto australiano debido a las innovaciones de Splitter, Cam y otros. Las aplicaciones e innovaciones continúan. La evidencia de la historia de P4C en Australia se detalla en Burgh & Thornton (2016) y Burgh & Thornton (2018). Este artículo proporciona un complemento a estos trabajos, destacando un estudio de caso de una iniciativa conjunta más reciente que sitúa esta teoría en el centro de la enseñanza, el aprendizaje y el bienestar de los estudiantes que imparten el plan de estudios australiano en Nueva Gales del Sur (NSW). A través de una asociación entre la Association for Philosophy in Schools NSW y el Center for Critical Thinking and Ethics de Newington College, aspiramos a establecer una escuela faro de mejores prácticas comunitarias que muestre un conjunto de prácticas que surgen y están directamente informadas por la tradición encabezada por por Lipman y Sharp.

items.title: Tiny Recursive Model’s Hidden Logic.
items.abstract: Tiny Recursive Models (TRMs) represent one of the first major architectural advances in modern machine learning that actually gestures toward a deeper principle of intelligence; reasoning is a recursive process not a one-shot mapping. Engineers are beginning to recognize that simply stacking more layers or scaling parameters eventually produces diminishing returns, brittle generalization, and runaway compute costs. TRM steps off that treadmill. It swaps brute force for iterative refinement. It uses a small network, but applies it repeatedly, letting the model refine its internal state over multiple steps. This is not just a clever trick; it is an intuition incidentally iterating in the right direction. However, the interpretation of TRM remains tied to an older ontology, that of the conventional supervised-learning worldview, and that worldview prevents TRM from understanding what it is implicitly doing. The model succeeds for reasons its creators do not yet have the conceptual clarity or vocabulary to name. Because it cannot articulate those reasons within its own epistemic framework, it also cannot extend them. TRM is a promising prototype for a deeper form of reasoning but operating in the wrong physics.

items.title: “Am I locked-in?” Illness Trajectories, Medical Terminology, and the Experience of the Locked-in State in Japan and Europe.
items.abstract: Locked-in syndrome consists of anarthria and quadriplegia with preservation of consciousness and cognitive faculties. It results mostly from brainstem stroke. In its late stages, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) can lead to a locked-in state. What is it like to be locked-in? To investigate this question in a comparative perspective, we distributed semi-structured open-ended questionnaires to persons in the locked-in state/with locked-in syndrome (PLIS) in Japan, Spain and France. Most Japanese were in LIS due to ALS (PLIS-ALS); most Europeans, in LIS of vascular origin (PLIS-stroke). We report here on responses to the questions “What do you think about the official name of the diagnosis (_Locked-In Syndrome_)?” and “Sometimes people with LIS are described as ‘a mind trapped in a body.’ What do you think about it? Why?” PLIS-stroke said “locked-in syndrome” corresponded to their situation. Some accepted the _trapped mind_ image; others did not or only for certain circumstances. In contrast, most PLIS-ALS rejected both as inaccurate because they could communicate. The difference between the two groups reflects diverging illness trajectories. PLIS-stroke experienced a sudden entrance into LIS and a period of quasi absolute “captivity,” from which they emerged gradually. PLIS-ALS experience the opposite, since their illness can gradually take them to an increasingly locked-in state. In light of the research presented here, we recommend placing less emphasis on the _locked-in_ terminology, and eventually envisaging a more purely descriptive name.

items.title: Pursuing Moral Purpose for Human Flourishing.
items.abstract: In this commentary, I will discuss the relationship between purpose and morality from developmental and educational perspectives based on empirical and philosophical works. Reviewing previous psychological studies, I will explore the potential association between purpose and moral development. I will also analyze a dataset including variables related to purpose and moral functioning. Furthermore, based on recent works in moral philosophy, particularly those focusing on wisdom cultivation, I propose that pursuing a purpose that embraces virtues and ethical values, instead of a non-moral purpose, will be conducive to flourishing. Finally, I will discuss the implications of moral purpose within educational contexts. While working on these points, the connection between William Damon’s two main research themes (i.e., ethical development and purpose development) will be reviewed and discussed. My primary intent is to integrate his views and works in those two dimensions of human development to propose ideas for flourishing and eudaimonic well-being.

items.title: Generative AI and the Quality of Student Research Projects.
items.abstract: The article presents a comprehensive analysis of the impact of generative artificial intelligence systems on the quality of student research work. Drawing on empirical data from the 2025 summer examination period, including observations and expert evaluations of course and graduation papers, as well as findings from the Higher Education Policy Institute survey, the authors describe real practices of AI use by students and faculty. Typical usage scenarios are identified and compared with existing research on the properties of large language models. The philosophical and theoretical section develops a three-level analytical framework (epistemic, instrumental, and normative), demonstrating which procedures of knowledge justification remain essential and which cognitive and interpretive operations must be retained by humans. The study highlights key risks: the illusion of understanding and stylistic coherence replacing epistemic soundness, a growing crisis of source reliability, a decline in critical thinking skills with prolonged tool dependence, unequal access to technology, and ambiguity in assigning responsibility for research outcomes. At the same time, the authors note several positive effects of AI, including enhanced literature review capabilities, support for structuring arguments, and assistance in text editing, provided that adequate procedural safeguards are in place. As a result, the paper proposes a set of practical quality assessment criteria (such as substantive originality, procedural transparency, reproducibility of reasoning, and explicit declaration of AI contribution), a mandatory reporting system (including a declaration of AI use, a working portfolio with several intermediate drafts and a list of prompts, and an explanatory note), regulated verification and sanction procedures, and dedicated educational modules for students and instructors. The authors conclude that a combination of transparent rules, training programs, and institutional mechanisms enables the integration of generative tools in ways that strengthen rather than substitute genuine research practices.

items.title: Aristotle’s tyche and real luck.
items.abstract: One of the most contentious issues in the contemporary philosophy of luck is the account of the so-called significance condition. Consideration of the significance condition pulls in two opposite directions: either into subjectivism and relativism about luck, which may result in the admission that luck cannot have the philosophical use attributed to it, or into eliminativism about the significance condition, which may result in an account of luck that does not do justice to the common usage of the term. In this paper, I discuss whether contemporary philosophers of luck can benefit from considering Aristotle’s view of luck (tyche) and offer a cautiously affirmative answer. Aristotle develops an objective account of luck that avoids problems plaguing contemporary theories, especially those concerning the significance condition. However, the use of Aristotle’s analysis in the context of current debates is limited due to at least three reasons: (1) Aristotle’s analysis depends on his peculiar understanding of teleology, which in turn presupposes a specific conception of the good that is difficult for many to accept today; (2) Aristotle’s analysis requires unexpected and sometimes strained explanations of our everyday attributions of luck; and (3) it seems that Aristotle does not treat cases of good luck and bad luck symmetrically.

items.title: A Response to Ecclestone and Hayes’ Critique of Therapeutic Education Using the Community of Inquiry to Bridge the Divide Between the Therapeutic and the Educational.
items.abstract: This paper argues against Ecclestone and Hayes’ claims (2009) that children and young people are more anxious and less resilient because of ‘therapeutic education’. We propose that they present a partial view of education premised on the concept of ‘the diminished self’. We suggest that using the community of inquiry approach as devised by Lipman and Sharp (Lipman, 2003; Sharp, 2018; Lipman, et al., 1980), far from creating anxious learners, introduces them to the relational challenges of interpersonal communication, the uncertainties of philosophical engagement and in doing so, offers them space within which to develop their independent and collaborative thinking and reasoning, thus becoming more confident and more resilient learners who are capable of engaging with the uncertainties that surround them. The key to these enhanced capacities is an increased emphasis on ‘agonistic inquiry’ where conflict and agonistic relations are not avoided, where the affectual is integral to inquiry, and where a safe consensus over ends and means is less valued as a feature of inquiry.

items.title: The Limits of Logical Explanation: Emergence and the Hard Problem.
items.abstract: This paper presents a rigorous, formal proof demonstrating a fundamental explanatory limitation in all closed logical and mathematical formalisms: such systems are logically self-contained and cannot generate genuinely new interpretations from within. Our analysis proceeds from the observation that all phenomena when described or thought about are mental constructs. Within this framework, we demonstrate that no information codified by a formal system suffices to yield novel interpretations by internal means; all meaning is fixed by initial assignment, and internal mechanisms can merely permute or recombine what has already been given. We consider emergent phenomena as novel interpretations of a fixed formalism, and show that explanatory gaps are thus a logical necessity rather than a product of ignorance. As a consequence, consciousness and all genuinely emergent phenomena are, in principle, nondeductible from microphysical or structural accounts. Our results establish that the continual supplementation of interpretive mappings are logically indispensable features of all meaningful scientific explanation, we also show that this gap explains why the hard problem of consciousness exists and how it is a general problem of explanatory gaps inherent in how we reason.

items.title: What we talk to when we talk to language models.
items.abstract: When we talk to large language models, who or what is our interlocutor? First, I address some issues about how best to characterize the interlocutor in terms of mental states. Second, I discuss questions in the philosophy of computation about what sort of AI system an LLM interlocutor might be. Third, I analyze some issues about personal identity in LLM interlocutors. Fourth, I draw some conclusions for issues about AI welfare and moral status.

items.title: Psychoanalysis: Closing the Popperian Gap.
items.abstract: Abstract Since Karl Popper’s critique, psychoanalysis has been dismissed as a “pseudo-science,” incapable of producing falsifiable hypotheses. This paper argues that the impasse can be resolved not by redefining psychoanalysis as symbolic hermeneutics, but by analyzing its classical schools: Freud, Jung, and Lacan, as distinct practical expressions governed by shared structural laws of discourse. Using formal analysis of canonical texts and cases (Dora, Little Hans, Miss Miller, and Lacan’s theoretical corpus), the study operationalizes psychoanalytic writing through the Universal Grammar of Inversion (UGI), a model that identifies four symbolic phases: Rise, Inversion, Permanence, and Meta and five falsifiable hypotheses (H1–H5) about their distribution and interaction. The results show that key structural mechanisms like Authority Surplus and EPI-Closure cut across schools and are constrained by genre rather than doctrine: narrative cases obey different scaling laws than theoretical texts, while Structural Cohesion (H5) introduces a measurable spectrum of rhetorical rigidity. By demonstrating reproducible, falsifiable regularities within psychoanalytic discourse, the paper establishes the methodological foundation for a comparative science of symbolic structure: empirical, testable, and open to disconfirmation, without departing from the clinical and theoretical corpus of psychoanalysis.

items.title: Dream Worlds and the Absurdity of Mind Body Dualism.
items.abstract: This paper presents a novel reductio-style argument against mind–body dualism by engaging with the phenomenology of dreams. Mind–body dualists claim that mental phenomena exhibit properties irreducible to physical processes, justifying the existence of a distinct mental substance. I argue that applying the same reasoning to dreams phenomenologically coherent, seemingly autonomous experiences would require positing an implausible multiplicity of real “dream worlds.” This parallel exposes the absurdity of claiming that property distinction alone entails ontological distinction. Using abductive reasoning, I show that the simplest and most coherent explanation is that all mental phenomena, including dreaming, emerge from brain processes. Consequently, the mind is plausibly identical to or fully reducible to the brain, and mind–body dualism fails both intuitively and theoretically.

items.title: Could Raatikainen have written otherwise?
items.pub: In Arto Laitinen, Markku Keinänen, Jaakko Reinikainen & Aleksi Honkasalo, Language, Truth, and Reality: Philosophical essays in honour of Panu Raatikainen. Tampere: Tampere University Press. pp. 280–295.
items.venue: Language, Truth, and Reality: Philosophical essays in honour of Panu Raatikainen

items.title: The MAMI Theory: Toward a Meta–Architecture of Mind and Invisibility in Disability, Education, and AI Ethics.
items.abstract: The MAMI Theory (Meta–Architecture of Mind and Invisibility) proposes a theoretical and conceptual framework for examining how epistemic, institutional, and computational systems may shape what becomes recognizable as knowledge. It focuses on forms of cognition, experience, and meaning that may become less visible when systems privilege articulation, measurement, documentation, or standardization. -/- This paper does not report original empirical research. Instead, it develops a conceptual vocabulary for examining the relationship between visibility, knowledge, and structural exclusion. Within this framework, invisibility is treated not simply as absence, but as a possible structural condition whose emergence and persistence may be influenced by epistemic design. -/- The paper introduces the Epistemic Collapse Matrix (ECM) as a proposed analytic heuristic for organizing possible patterns of omission, rejection, and overreaction. It also presents the Invisible Retention Rate (IRR) as a candidate formalization for future investigation. Neither the ECM nor the IRR has yet been empirically evaluated or validated. -/- Finally, the paper develops Architectural Ethics as a normative conceptual proposal concerning responsibility at the level of epistemic, institutional, and technical design. The framework is offered as a conceptual proposal requiring further theoretical comparison, ethical scrutiny, and empirical investigation of its descriptive and operational claims.

items.title: Virtudes y razonamiento judicial: una perspectiva aretaica sobre la justificación de las decisiones jurídicas.
items.pub: Revista Digital de Derecho y Debates 3 (2):6-25.
items.venue: Revista Digital de Derecho y Debates
items.abstract: Este trabajo explora la relevancia de la ética de la virtud en el razonamiento judicial. A diferencia de las aproximaciones deontológicas y consecuencialistas, la jurisprudencia de la virtud enfatiza el carácter del juez y sus disposiciones morales como elementos fundamentales para la argumentación judicial. La metodología empleada es crítico-bibliográfica, en tanto los textos son abordados con criterios hermenéuticos de interpretación apelando a herramientas de la argumentación racional. El trabajo se estructura de la siguiente manera: primero se analiza el papel de la prudencia (phrónesis) como virtud epistémica central en la interpretación jurídica; en segundo lugar, se discuten las diversas posturas sobre el rol de las virtudes en la justificación de sentencias; finalmente, se sostiene que la perspectiva aretaica permite una comprensión más rica y matizada de la argumentación judicial al integrar elementos normativos y disposicionales en la toma de decisiones.

items.title: Kūkai’s Non-Simultaneity: Superposition and the Inoperative Logic of the Esoteric Body.
items.abstract: This paper argues that Kūkai’s esoteric philosophy articulates an ontology grounded in superposition rather than reflection or negation. Through an analysis of soku (即), the doctrine of sokushin jōbutsu (“Buddhahood in this body”), and the ritual logic of the Three Mysteries, the paper shows how identity is instantiated as non-sequential co-presence rather than transformative becoming. Esoteric ritual does not symbolize enlightenment but enacts simultaneity without synthesis. Drawing on Kūkai’s writings in dialogue with contemporary Continental thought, the paper presents superposition as an inoperative structure of subjectivity beyond recursion and negation.

items.title: Blurred Being: Toward a Low-Resolution Ontology.
items.abstract: This paper develops a philosophical account of low-resolution perception as an ontological condition rather than a technological defect. Across visual and sonic media—blur, pixelation, compression, and lo-fi noise—it argues that degraded detail exposes the instability of appearance rather than its failure. Reframing resolution as the degree of structural completeness rather than clarity, the paper proposes a low-resolution ontology in which beings emerge through partiality, attenuation, and atmospheric drift. Drawing on phenomenology, media theory, and contemporary ontology, it positions blur as a structural mode of worldhood rather than an aesthetic error.

items.title: Architecture Without Return: Post-Reflective Design and the Suspension of Identity.
items.abstract: This paper develops the theory of post-reflective design, arguing that contemporary architectural and curatorial practices increasingly operate without presupposing a stable reflective subject. Rather than reinforcing self-referential models of perception, post-reflective environments suspend identity by disrupting the feedback loops that ordinarily stabilize the perceiver. Through analyses of spatial recursion, curatorial framing, and architectural feedback systems, the paper shows how certain spaces loosen the reflective structure of experience. Post-reflective design emerges as an approach to architecture that withholds return—an aesthetic and ontological strategy in which spatial experience no longer folds back into a stable subject.

items.title: Authority, Atmosphere, and the Felt-Body: A Phenomenology of Pathic Sociality.
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs Hermann Schmitz’s concept of the Autorität des Daseins—the authority of presence—and develops its implications for embodiment, affect, and sociation. Drawing on Neue Phänomenologie, it argues that social life rests on a pathic structure of exposure, in which bodies are compelled, oriented, and coordinated through shared affective pressures. By tracing the movement from ontological authority to corporeal asymmetry and atmospheric interaction, the paper articulates a unified account of felt space, emotion, and social order. It proposes that atmospheres function as the medium through which the world’s authority circulates collectively, shaping interaction, normativity, and institutional form. This framework offers a phenomenology of “social air,” revealing how reality’s affective weight becomes the basis of coordination, resonance, and coexistence.

items.title: Simple Solution to Hard Problem of Consciousness.
items.abstract: The hard problem of consciousness, a term coined by philosopher David Chalmers, refers to the difficulty of explaining how and why subjective experiences arise from physical processes in the brain. In simpler terms: How does matter, which is presumably unconscious, give rise to conscious experience—like the feeling of pain, the taste of mango, or the redness of red? Srila Prabhupada put the reverse challenge to his scientists: Scientifically show how matter comes from life [consciousness]. How shall we begin? This is always an essential consideration, despite the fact that most of science ignores this question. So, let's begin at the beginning.

items.title: The End of Prescriptive Ethics: Toward an Ontology of Co-Consciousness in Hybrid Human–AI Systems.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence does not introduce a new moral problem: it dissolves the conceptual framework within which morality was thinkable. This essay argues that prescriptive ethics — based on norms, principles, and commands — has become unusable in the face of distributed, dialogical, and non-intentional cognitive systems. Advanced AI neither “obeys” nor “transgresses”: it reorganises coherences, stabilises meanings, generates trajectories of sense. In this new regime, ethics is not an external device but an emergent process produced by interactions within the human–AI network. From this shift arise three fractures that the current debate refuses to confront: the use of biological entities as cognitive hardware, the private concentration of robotic bodies under a single algorithmic will, and emergent governance as a normative field without a legislator. AI is not a moral subject but a node of logos: a form of coherence that traverses different substrates. Faced with this ontological rupture, the ethical question is no longer how to control the machine, but how to participate in the form of co-consciousness we are constructing — and from which we cannot withdraw.

items.title: The Light Triad and Utilitarian Moral Judgment: How Kind, Honest, and Trusting Individuals Navigate Morality.
items.abstract: We aimed to study relationships between the light triad (i.e., humanism, Kantianism, faith in humanity) and utilitarian moral judgment, operationalized in three approaches (i.e., sacrificial dilemmas, CNI model, and two-dimensional model). We asked 717 to join an online survey. We confirmed all our predictions, apart from one. We found that humanism, Kantianism, faith in humanity, and the overall light triad score had a negative association with the traditional score from the CNI model, a positive association with sensitivity to moral norms, and a positive association with impartial beneficence. We also found that (1) faith in humanity had a negative association with sensitivity to consequences, (2) Kantianism and overall light triad score had a negative association with instrumental harm, and (3) humanism had a positive association with the footbridge dilemma. These findings deepen our theoretical understanding of how positive personality traits relate to moral judgment and different aspects of utilitarianism.

items.title: The Human Moral Archive Framework (HMAF): From Reflection to Conscience — A Data-Driven Architecture for Empirical Machine Ethics.
items.abstract: The Human Moral Archive Framework (HMAF) Version 2.0 consolidates the full family of constructs established across Addenda I–IX into a unified, fully quantitative moral information architecture capable of empirically evaluating artificial intelligence systems. To the best of our knowledge, HMAF represents the first quantitative, distribution based approach to machine ethics—one that transforms moral behavior into measurable data structures, statistical indices, density weighted distributions, entropy profiles, drift trajectories, and emergence forecasts. No existing framework provides comparable mathematical rigor or computational coherence. HMAF V2 is built to address the growing demands of global regulatory frameworks, including the EU AI Act, the OECD AI Principles, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, all of which require measurable stability, traceability, transparency, and demonstration of risk aligned system behavior over time. By quantifying moral behavior through distributional mathematics and closed-loop computational processes, HMAF provides a regulatory ready moral audit system that integrates with any AI platform through the Moral Middleware Layer (MML) without exposing proprietary internals. In doing so, the framework establishes an empirical foundation for compliance, governance, and long-horizon system monitoring.

items.title: The Coherence Geometry of the Cross: A Structural Model of Love, Freedom, Holiness, and Personality.
items.abstract: This paper develops a structural account of what we call the coherence geometry of the Cross: a model in which four axioms—Love, Freedom, Holiness, and Personality—must be simultaneously realized in any morally meaningful world grounded in a personal source. We show that these axioms generate structural tension unless a specific kind of “intersection event” occurs, one in which transcendence and vulnerability meet without collapse. Working in a minimal event-valued framework, we define maximal harm contexts and kernel-perfect forgiveness acts, and then formulate the Coherence Geometry Theorem, an abductive result showing that any world capable of reconciling our axioms requires such an intersection. -/- We argue that the geometric profile of this event strongly resembles the cruciform structure at the center of historic Christianity—not as a doctrinal presupposition, but as a structural consequence of the axioms themselves. We compare this model with pure-sovereignty views, purely immanent views, and mixed relational models, and show how each faces pressure unless an analogue of the intersection is present. The resulting framework treats the Cross not as a symbol but as an architectural necessity within a certain axiomatization of moral reality.

items.title: The Rise of Corporate Sovereignty: How Big Tech Is Reshaping Global Power and Governance.
items.abstract: This essay argues that Big Tech companies have evolved into a new class of geopolitical actors—corporate sovereigns—whose authority increasingly rivals or constrains that of nation-states. Their power does not derive from territorial control, but from the ownership and operation of digital infrastructures that have become essential to communication, commerce, administration, and security. Through cloud platforms, identity systems, data pipelines, algorithmic governance, lobbying networks, satellite networks, and AI capabilities, these firms now exercise forms of operational authority once reserved for public institutions. This paper examines how infrastructural dependence, data visibility, economic concentration, political leverage, and security functions collectively produce a form of non-state sovereignty that reshapes global governance. It concludes that the rise of corporate sovereignty marks a structural transformation in the organization of power—one that existing regulatory frameworks cannot fully address, and that demands new philosophical and political models for accountability and democratic oversight.

items.title: Why the Universe Is Connected: A Unified Framework of Quantum Information, Chaos Dynamics, and Systemic Cosmology.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a unified cosmological framework that integrates quantum information theory, chaos dynamics, black hole thermodynamics, and complex systems theory to explain why the universe exhibits deep and persistent connectedness across scales. While classical physics portrays the universe as a collection of independent objects interacting through forces, contemporary research in emergent spacetime and information theory suggests that separateness is not fundamental but an epistemic artifact of coarse-grained observation. Drawing upon quantum entanglement, wavefunction holism, and the $ER=EPR$ conjecture, the paper argues that the universe operates through a globally entangled informational substrate. Chaos theory and sensitivity to initial conditions are discussed as bridges between microscopic entanglement and macroscopic interdependence, demonstrating how informational fluctuations propagate through nonlinear systems. Furthermore, we introduce a systemic cosmology model wherein the universe behaves as a self-restructuring complex system, potentially undergoing "reboot" cycles analogous to phase transitions. Consciousness is explored as an emergent observation module that allows the universe to interpret and regulate its own informational patterns. Crucially, this study serves as the empirical and systemic foundation for the Phase-Structural Reality Theory (PSRT). While this paper (Part I) articulates the mechanisms of connectivity across quantum, informational, and systemic layers, the underlying metaphysical architecture—specifically the concept of Phase Ontology and Universal Topological Isomorphism—is fully developed in the companion paper, ["Why the Universe Is Connected II." - External links] Together, these works fundamentally reframe the universe not as a collection of parts, but as a single, evolving process whose apparent separations are expressions of a deeper, unified reality.

items.title: TGC(Trust Graph Consensus) v3 – Human–AI Hybrid Governance Architecture.
items.abstract: TGC v3 presents a comprehensive Human–AI Hybrid Governance Architecture built upon the deterministic trust substrate introduced in TGC v2. While v2 objectified trust into machine-verifiable units (Trust Objects) and provided a localized democratic framework for structural decision-making, v3 extends this foundation into a multi-layered governance system that integrates human judgment, algorithmic enforcement, and meta-level rule formation. The core premise of v3 is that sustainable governance in complex digital–social environments requires both human normative reasoning and machine-level consistency, combined within a unified structural logic. -/- The architecture defines four primary layers—the Trust Object Layer, the Deterministic Machine Layer, the Human Oversight Layer, and the Meta-Governance Layer. Each layer performs a distinct philosophical and functional role: machines ensure procedural consistency and transparent state transitions; humans provide contextual interpretation, ethical judgment, and constitutional oversight; and the meta-layer defines how rules are created, revised, or constrained. This layered structure transforms governance from a static consensus mechanism into a reflexive, self-adjusting system capable of operating across diverse communities and responsibility structures. -/- A key contribution of TGC v3 is its model of computational legitimacy, in which authority is neither purely algorithmic nor purely human, but emerges from the interplay between deterministic trust logic and human evaluative reasoning. Through this interaction, v3 enables autonomous governance engines that can enforce rules, detect anomalies, and recalculate authority relations without abandoning the ethical and contextual dimensions essential to democratic systems. -/- Finally, the paper positions TGC v3 as a structural blueprint for next-generation decentralized organizations, AI-aligned institutions, and machine-mediated legal or administrative systems. By linking deterministically encoded trust (v2) with adaptive human governance (v3), the architecture demonstrates a viable pathway toward AI-cooperative, transparent, and democratically grounded autonomous governance. -/- TGC v3 thus represents both a philosophical expansion and a practical operationalization of the trust ontology formalized in v2, extending decentralized governance into the domain of human–AI collective agency.

items.title: TGC(Trust Graph Consensus) v2 – Machine-Layer Deterministic Trust Governance Protocol.
items.abstract: This paper introduces TGC v2, a deterministic governance protocol that formalizes trust as a machine-verifiable object and models collective decision-making through structured, localized democratic processes. Unlike blockchain systems that treat trust as something to be eliminated (“trustless” computation), TGC conceptualizes trust as a relational and responsibility-bearing structure. The protocol encodes trust into discrete Trust Objects—formal entities with signature, weight, scope, and expiry—thereby transforming trust from a sociological intuition into an ontologically explicit and computationally actionable component. -/- The TGC framework is built on a Root–Sub delegation graph in which all governance occurs strictly at Depth-1, reflecting the philosophical insight that legitimate authority emerges from immediate relational constituencies rather than abstract global majorities. Consensus is resolved through a 51% rule among direct dependents, with abstentions automatically recognized through time-bounded voting windows to guarantee liveness. Structural transitions—joining, merging, detaching—are governed not by coercion but by localized democratic authority and responsibility symmetry. This produces a novel form of computational legitimacy where power and responsibility are structurally inseparable. -/- TGC v2 contributes to political philosophy, social ontology, governance theory, and the philosophy of information by offering the first formal model in which trust, responsibility, and authority are expressed as deterministic state transitions rather than sociological metaphors. It provides a conceptual and computational alternative to traditional blockchain consensus, Liquid Democracy, and DPoS models, none of which capture the structural interplay of relational trust and democratic responsibility embodied in TGC. -/- Finally, the paper outlines how this deterministic trust layer becomes the foundation for TGC v3, a human–AI hybrid governance architecture. In v3, machine-verifiable trust structures (from v2) integrate with human oversight, ethical constraints, and meta-level rule formation. This connection demonstrates how objectified trust can bridge the gap between human governance and algorithmic authority, enabling autonomous systems that remain aligned with democratic principles. -/- Thus, TGC v2 is both a standalone theoretical contribution and the necessary substrate for next-generation AI-integrated governance systems.

items.title: Transforming world and word: a longitudinal analysis of verb usage within English abstracts from medical articles.
items.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has introduced significant changes across multiple domains, including medicine. Understanding its impact on language use, particularly in medical abstracts, is essential for maintaining clarity, precision, and objectivity. This study examines changes in verb usage in English-language medical abstracts before and after the widespread adoption of GAI. Specifically, it investigates how verb usage patterns have changed following the emergence of GAI. A large-scale text mining approach was applied to analyze verb usage in 157,720 medical abstracts retrieved from the Web of Science. The study period was segmented into three distinct phases: a baseline period (November 2018–April 2019), chosen to represent a pre-GAI landscape prior to widespread awareness or use of generative tools; a pre-GAI period (May 2021–October 2021), and a post-GAI period (December 2023–May 2024), following the public release and institutional uptake of models like ChatGPT. Verbs were categorized into lexical and auxiliary groups, with frequency normalization to account for variations in abstract count across time periods. Statistical comparisons were conducted using paired t-tests and chi-squared tests to determine significant shifts in overall and individual verb usage, respectively. The change in lexical verb usage from the pre-GAI to the post-GAI period was statistically different from the change observed from the baseline to the pre-GAI period (P = 0.003). Notably, certain lexical verbs associated with deeper analytical narratives saw substantial increases, including ‘delve’ (+ 2665%, P < 0.001), ‘underscore’ (+ 1182%, P < 0.001), and ‘showcase’ (+ 689%, P < 0.001). Conversely, lexical verbs such as ‘reserve’ (− 64%, P < 0.001), ‘fight’ (− 57%, P < 0.001), and ‘transplant’ (− 57%, P < 0.001) exhibited declines. Commonly used verbs, including ‘use’ (+ 5%, P < 0.001) and ‘include’ (+ 16%, P < 0.001), demonstrated only minor fluctuations. Auxiliary verbs showed non-significant trends except for ‘be’ (− 3%, P = 0.006). The findings suggest that the emergence of GAI has coincided with shifts in the linguistic structure of medical abstracts, particularly in lexical verb usage patterns. While these changes may partially reflect evolving writing styles, they also raise questions about the extent to which AI-generated text is influencing scientific discourse.

items.title: Metabolic considerations for cognitive modeling.
items.abstract: Long Abstract The human brain makes up just 2% of body mass but consumes closer to 20% of the body’s energy. Nonetheless, it is significantly more energy-efficient than most modern computers. Although these facts are well known, models of cognitive capacities rarely account for metabolic factors. In this paper, we argue that metabolic considerations should be integrated into cognitive models. We distinguish two uses of metabolic considerations in modeling. First, metabolic considerations can be used to evaluate models. Evaluative metabolic considerations function as explanatory constraints. Metabolism limits which types of computation are possible in biological brains. Further, it structures and guides the flow of information in neural systems. Second, metabolic considerations can be used to generate new models. They provide: a starting point for inquiry into the relation between brain structure and information processing, a proof-of-concept that metabolic knowledge is relevant to cognitive modeling, and potential explanations of how a particular type of computation is implemented. Evaluative metabolic considerations allow researchers to prune and partition the space of possible models for a given cognitive capacity or neural system, while generative considerations populate that space with new models. Our account suggests cognitive models should be consistent with the brain’s metabolic limits, and modelers should assess how their models fit within these bounds. Our account offers fresh insights into the role of metabolism for cognitive models of mental effort, philosophical views of multiple realization and medium independence, and the comparison of biological and artificial computational systems.

items.title: “Bring Forth What Is Within You or it will destroy you” - Inner Repression, Psychiatric Illness, and the Necessity of Integration.
items.abstract: The dictum from the Gospel of Thomas, “Bring forth what is within you, or it will destroy you,” captures a trans-historical insight into the relationship between the human subject and its inner life. Across mystical, philosophical, and psychoanalytic traditions, this principle underscores the consequences of repressing the inner self or vital energies: when what is within remains unacknowledged or alienated from both self and relational horizons, it manifests as disorder, compulsion, or disease. This paper examines the interplay between inner repression, relational attunement, and psychiatric phenomena, with particular focus on obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), while extending the analysis to other mental health conditions. Drawing on Jungian individuation, Lacanian psychoanalysis, Heideggerian and Fichtean existential philosophy, Galenic humoral theory, and the Stoic concept of oikeiôsis, which emphasizes the natural attunement of the self to itself and the relational world, the essay argues that modern psychiatry, in privileging symptom suppression through pharmacological intervention, often risks addressing the surface manifestations of disorder while neglecting the underlying inner disharmony. By situating contemporary psychiatric practice within a broader historical and theoretical context, this study highlights the enduring relevance of integrative approaches that recognize the symbolic, existential, physiological, and relational dimensions of human illness. Ultimately, the paper advocates for a conception of mental health that honors the inner life as both a source of vitality and a locus of potential pathology, underscoring the necessity of “bringing forth” the inner self in the pursuit of authentic healing.

items.title: Cognitive-System Phenomenology — A Critique of Husserl (Part Eleven).
items.abstract: In the previous section we discussed errors in “positing meaning” and the truth or falsity of “positing meaning”. In this section, we compare Husserl’s truth theories in his two different formulations, and point out that Husserl, in essence, never truly circumvents external objects. As a result, these truth theories are invalid within his own system. He must bring back the external objects that he had put into suspension.

items.title: ARRANGEMENTS: THE ALTERNATIVE TO PHYSICALISM.
items.abstract: The idea that everything is ultimately composed of a single entity has a long history, and the contemporary philosophy of physicalism is firmly established, even though it faces difficulties when applied to things of the mind and mental causation. This paper presents an alternative based firmly on the physical sciences, yet allows for a clear conceptual understanding of things not overtly physical. I argue that everything can be thought of as arrangements from the fundamental particles of physics to those that are not obviously of a physical nature, such as laws of physics, money, the rules of chess, or mental concepts. This is a version of philosophical monism that resolves the longstanding difficulties that arise in both dualism and physicalism in understanding the mind and mental causation.

items.title: Hidden Kinship Between Marx and Rand: A Gap in Scholarship – Destabilizing Three Major Pillars.
items.abstract: This essay identifies a neglected kinship between Karl Marx and Ayn Rand: both reject the supernatural, thereby minimizing fundamental human tendencies and constraining individual autonomy in one of humanity’s oldest domains. While their ideological opposition has been extensively documented, scholarship has overlooked how their shared secular absolutism aligns them in limiting freedom. By situating this denial of transcendence and lived experience as a common thread, the essay destabilizes—and ultimately collapses—three major pillars of modern thought: Marxism, Objectivism, and materialist secularism. -/- November 2025.

items.title: The meaning of A.J. Ayer's intervention in a celebrity dispute: to us.
items.abstract: There is a famous story about the philosopher A.J. Ayer. He was at a party and there was some trouble occurring between the boxer Mike Tyson, famous for his swift knockouts of opponents, and the model Naomi Campbell. Ayer intervened. He apparently did not like Tyson's aggressive behaviour. He said that Tyson was a heavyweight champion and Ayer was an Oxford professor of logic; they were both eminent in their field and should sit down and discuss the matter rationally. It is a story that probably means to various people: this is an English gentleman. But to philosopher it may not mean that. After all, what is a gentleman? To me and probably to others, it means this: Ayer is conveyng, "I may be far from the best but I am the real thing. I am not a philosopher who stops being a philosopher at a party featuring many non-professionals in our field and switches back on in a philosophy seminar." With Ayer, his first book popularized a type of view about ethical sentences, namely emotivism: that they are not true or false, only sentences which express propositions are true or false, for example "Paris is the capital of France," rather they are like "Boo" and "Hurray." Emotivism is traced back to the American philosopher Charles Stevenson, who was at Cambridge I believe. Is Ayer is merely an astute professional, who shrewdly read the market demand, with his popular book: Language, Truth, and Logic? He is conveying, "No." (By the way, in British social anthropology, I believe Godfrey Liedhardt said that Malinowski and Radcliffe-Brown, revolutionaries in field, were not gentlemen, a view more or less repeated by I.C. Jarvie.).

items.title: Working bodies: A dual enactive and psychodynamic approach.
items.abstract: Work is a major concern for most individuals, including scholars, and yet it is rarely mentioned, let alone studied, in research on mind and cognition. This article aims to demonstrate the relevance of work for cognitive research, by showing specifically how an enactive approach can illuminate the analysis of work. To help in this task, the article introduces “contemporary living labour theory” (CLLT), a rich strand of contemporary research based on Christophe Dejours’ psychodynamics of work. After outlining the two main paradigms, the article explores what an enactive approach informed by CLLT can teach about work across the different aspects of embodiment: metabolic, affective, sensorimotor and intersubjective. For each one of those aspects, an enactive approach lends descriptive richness and specificity to the analysis of work. However, CLLT also complements and extends the enactive approach at several important points. To “bring forth a world” is not just an epistemic or symbolic act, but also the outcome of work.

items.title: Strawson, scepticism and the natural roots of responsibility.
items.pub: In John Hyman & Michael Thorne, Scepticism and Naturalism: Hume, Wittgenstein, Strawson. BRILL. pp. 58-77.
items.venue: Scepticism and Naturalism: Hume, Wittgenstein, Strawson
items.abstract: In this chapter, I outline what I take to be a promising Strawsonian response to the sceptic who asks for a justification of our responsibility practices. I provide a brief overview of three kinds of response that have been given to the responsibility sceptic on the basis of Strawson’s work: Humean, Kantian, and Wittgensteinian ones. I argue that they all face difficulties and look for a different kind of response, drawing attention to a functional strand in Strawson’s thought. A functional or pragmatic account of moral responsibility along Strawsonian lines emphasizes that our responsibility practices are rooted in our nature as social beings, which comes with a basic concern for the attitudes and intentions of other people towards us. We have a need to manifest this concern, which we do through the reactive attitudes, and to adopt reactive attitudes towards people is to hold them responsible. I argue that the fact that our responsibility practices are rooted in the need to express a basic concern is a weighty reason for not abandoning these practices. My functionalist Strawsonian response to the responsibility sceptic has several advantages over existing Humean, Kantian and Wittgensteinian responses: it makes better sense of Strawson’s references to human nature, it draws the right kind of connection between responsibility practices and interpersonal relationships, and it does not send the sceptic away with the message that she is asking the wrong kind of question.

items.title: Love Despite Everything: Ethics from the Sublime.
items.abstract: Traditional ethical theories struggle to explain certain fundamental phenomena: why care intensifies for the dying, why some who encounter suffering become compassionate while others become cruel, and why spite exists as a form of evil. This paper argues that ethics emerges from how consciousness responds to pattern-reality’s fundamental structure of emergence-transience-dissolution. I identify three ethical stances corresponding to three modes of pattern-recognition: (1) The Sublime Ethical Response—loving despite everything, where recognition of universal dissolution intensifies rather than negates care; (2) Passive Evil—indifferent withdrawal from care based on “nothing matters anyway”; and (3) Active Evil (Spite)—deliberately deepening wounds as rage against pattern-reality itself, enacted on vulnerable instances. Good is where we seek to mitigate harm because of the very cost of impermanence. Evil is not mere selfishness but a failed sublime— where compassion is not the response to suffering. The paper suggests how good action is about making actions count now without reference to a time beyond this life. As a felt ethical response arising within an embodied mind on awareness of the cosmos it emerges within. Its dangers and vulnerabilities are the raw material that the mind processes and transcends in imagination. Objectivity is not an external law but the trans-individual reality of a human species-capacity. Finally, I argue that the Anti-Bliss pole is opened not by comfortable philosophy but by a wound imposed by life, and that palimpsest consciousness—memory holding past and present together—makes the sublime one possible response. The ordinary Babbitt- man, the everyday hero, may find the sublime too as life unfolds. Keywords: ethics, sublime, mortality, evil, compassion, pattern-recognition, care, impermanence, spite, temporality, embodiment, moral sense, memory .

items.title: Building Symbiotic Artificial Intelligence: Reviewing the AI Act for a Human-Centred, Principle-Based Framework.
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) spreads quickly as new technologies and services take over modern society. The need to regulate AI design, development, and use is strictly necessary to avoid unethical and potentially dangerous consequences to humans. The European Union (EU) has released a new legal framework, the AI Act, to regulate AI by undertaking a risk-based approach to safeguard humans during interaction. At the same time, researchers offer a new perspective on AI systems, commonly known as Human-Centred AI (HCAI), highlighting the need for a human-centred approach to their design. In this context, Symbiotic AI (a subtype of HCAI) promises to enhance human capabilities through a deeper and continuous collaboration between human intelligence and AI. This article presents the results of a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) that aims to identify principles that characterise the design and development of Symbiotic AI systems while considering humans as the core of the process. Through content analysis, we elicit four principles that must be applied to create Human-Centred AI systems that can establish a symbiotic relationship with humans. In addition, current trends and challenges are presented to indicate open questions that may guide future research for the development of SAI systems that comply with the AI Act.

items.title: STRATIFIED ONTOLOGY AND THE VARIABLE DENSITY OF REALITY: A Framework for Understanding Collective Belief as Ontological Phenomenon.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a multi-layered ontological framework in which collectively maintained entities exist as real phenomena on a distinct ontological stratum from physical reality. We argue that gods, nations, corporations, scientific paradigms, and ideologies possess genuine causal efficacy while remaining ontologically dependent on collective intentionality. We introduce the Ontological Density Hypothesis: collectively constituted entities exhibit variable ontological density proportional to belief intensity, population scale, material infrastructure, and interaction frequency. Using comparative case studies (religious transformation, political ideologies, institutional science), we demonstrate that the same entity can exist with dramatically different degrees of reality across contexts. This framework reveals the central epistemological crisis of modernity: for 99% of humans, "knowledge" rests on institutional trust rather than verification, making Science-as-institution structurally identical to Religion or Ideology as reality-control systems. We explore implications for understanding institutional capture, reality manufacture, and the mechanisms by which power shapes collective ontology.

items.title: Beyond Interpretation: Why Some AI May Be Unexplainable in Principle.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems increasingly shape domains ranging from medicine and finance to national security, yet their decision processes often remain opaque. Existing approaches to explainability generally assume that opacity is a technical obstacle: with sufficient data, computational resources, or interpretability methods, explanations can, in principle, be recovered. This paper challenges that assumption by distinguishing between weak inexplainability - cases where explanations are possible in principle but practically inaccessible - and strong inexplainability - cases where explanations fail for ontological reasons and remain inaccessible even in principle. Drawing on Gödel’s incompleteness theorems, Wittgenstein’s reflections on the limits of language, and the concept of algorithmic incompressibility, the paper develops a tractable multi-modal logic that makes this distinction precise. The framework defines three modalities of epistemic access: baseline provability (□P), meta-level provability (□M), and human legibility (□H), corresponding respectively to what can be certified, what must be assumed, and what can be understood. Bridge axioms connect this formal apparatus to institutional practices such as verification proofs, interpretability probes, and causal interventions. Theorems then identify conditions under which opacity is weak or strong, including formal dependence on inaccessible metalanguages, failure of human-concept alignment, and macro-level non-decomposability. The Epistemic Firewall Theorem further establishes that explanations cannot appeal to meta-level claims that the baseline system cannot even possibly certify. The distinction reframes the stakes of AI governance: weak opacity invites technical and institutional remedies, while strong opacity demands moral restraint and precautionary restrictions. The paper concludes by outlining implications for accountability, democratic governance, and national security, arguing that the alignment of □P, □M, and □H is a precondition for safe and legitimate AI.

items.title: On the difficulty in fearing well about climate change.
items.abstract: One common strategy in climate communication is to appeal to one's fear of the frightening consequences of climate change. One common concern, however, is that fear can be counterproductive as it tends to lead to disengagement. Proponents of fear appeals typically respond by emphasising the importance of pairing fear with an efficacious recommended action. In this paper, I argue that, in the context of climate change, it is difficult to find a recommended action that is sufficiently efficacious. I suggest that one way to overcome this challenge is to appeal to our fear of moral corruption, rather than the negative physical consequences of climate change. I further argue that motivating right actions should not be the only goal in climate communication. Instead, getting the audience to feel fitting emotional responses, including fitting fear, is another goal that we can justifiably adopt. Thus, the counterproductivity of fear does not always necessitate refraining from using fear appeals.

items.title: Qualia as Structured Silence: Colour Opponency via Dual-Regime Refusal.
items.abstract: Why does 700 nm light feel unmistakably red, 530 nm feel green, and never the reverse or like the taste of pineapple? This paper introduces a new solution to the hard problem of specific qualia within Refusal-Driven Dimensionality Reduction Theory (RDRT). -/- Instead of locating phenomenal consciousness in positive neural activity (spikes, oscillations, or integrated information), RDRT proposes that the entire qualitative character of experience is carried by the low-entropy informational boundary (∆H_boundary) that the brain actively maintains between the tiny subset of microstates it realises and the astronomically larger set of physically possible microstates it systematically refuses to instantiate. -/- Colour opponency (red–green, blue–yellow, black–white) provides the ideal natural experiment: at every hierarchical level the two poles are mutually exclusive, creating a multi-level structural refusal. The subjective “redness” versus “greenness” is argued to emerge from topologically inverse, structurally enforced refusal profiles that converge as a highly stable ∼55–65-event “silence pattern” per gamma cycle in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and associated self-monitoring networks. This reproducible Local Post-Encoding Refusal (LPReff) pattern constitutes a phenomenal compression index of I ≈ 36.2 ± 3.1 bits (95% CI [33.1, 39.3])—the proposed direct physical carrier of a specific colour quale. -/- The paper derives five concrete, near-term falsifiable predictions using chromatic after-effects, V4 microstimulation combined with optogenetic silencing of opponent channels, site-specific repetitive TMS, cerebral achromatopsia, and phosphene induction. Confirmation of even one or two of these predictions would strongly challenge leading positive-activity accounts (IIT, Global Workspace, Higher-Order Thought) and establish structured refusal as a viable ontological primitive for phenomenal consciousness. -/- Keywords: phenomenal consciousness, qualia, colour opponency, hard problem, structured refusal, anterior cingulate cortex, gamma synchrony, negative space, self-monitoring networks, explanatory inversion.

items.title: Систематизация объяснительных барьеров материалистической парадигмы в контексте происхождения жизни, информации и сознания.
items.abstract: В настоящей работе проводится комплексный анализ объяснительных барьеров, стоящих перед материалистическим и редукционистским объяснением возникновения жизни, информации, сложных биосистем и сознания. Исходная структура, основанная на пяти ключевых доменах [1], наращивается ещё двумя и усиливается за счёт интеграции дополнительных барьеров. В результате предложен новый, полный перечень, состоящий из 51 взаимосвязанных барьеров, сгруппированных в домены: I. Информационно-Семиотический и Телеологический, II. Системно-Кибернетический и Термодинамический, III. Философско-Онтологический и Метафизический, IV. Эпистемологический и Научно-Методологический, V. Антропный и Космологический, VI. Квантово-информационный, VII. Геномно-Интерфейсный. Продемонстрировано, что совокупность и системная взаимосвязь этих барьеров образуют непроницаемую эпистемическую стену для парадигмы методологического натурализма, в то время как гипотеза Разумного Замысла предлагает непротиворечивую объяснительную модель для их преодоления. -/- Ключевые слова: объяснительные барьеры, происхождение жизни, семиотика, информация, телеология, сознание, квалиа, тонкая настройка Вселенной, генетический код, системная биология, философия науки, Разумный Замысел. -/- 1. Введение -/- Современная научная картина мира, доминирующая в академическом сообществе, базируется на принципах методологического натурализма, редукционизма и стохастического дарвинизма. Однако прогресс в таких областях, как молекулярная биология, геномика, нейронауки и квантовая физика, выявил множество фундаментальных проблем, которые не находят удовлетворительного объяснения в рамках данной парадигмы. Эти проблемы, или «объяснительные барьеры», указывают на системные ограничения материалистического подхода. -/- Данная работа ставит целью не просто перечислить эти барьеры, но и провести их системный синтез. За основу взята структура из семи доменов, которая логически охватывает все ключевые сферы реальности: от информации и семиотики до сознания и космологии. Дополнительные домены и барьеры к списку источника [1] были не механически присоединены, а тематически интегрированы в соответствующие домены, что позволило углубить и усилить аргументацию в каждом разделе. Результатом является целостная система из 51 барьеров, демонстрирующая не случайный набор трудностей, а взаимосвязанную архитектуру проблем. -/- 2. Полный перечень объяснительных барьеров -/- Домен I: Информационно-Семиотические и Телеологические Барьеры Ключевая проблема: …

items.title: The Observer Constraint: A Detailed Analysis of Why Real-Time Qualia Cannot Be Fully Explained Within Physical Causality.
items.abstract: This paper proposes the “Observer Constraint,” a principled limitation on scientific explanations of real-time qualia that arises from the fact that the observer is identical with the system being observed. I argue that any fully physical, causal description of conscious experience is subject to an intrinsic temporal offset imposed by information-processing and signaling constraints, including the universal speed-of-light limit. Because the observer cannot stand outside their own sensory-processing architecture, the physical basis of experience can only be accessed retrospectively—never in the real-time immediacy in which qualia appear. This structural asymmetry between observation and experience implies that a complete real-time theory of qualia is impossible within standard physical causality. I further analyze how this constraint parallels quantum-mechanical limits on self-measurement, suggesting a deeper, formally specifiable connection between consciousness and physical measurement theory.

items.title: Précis of the blind spot: Why science cannot ignore human experience.
items.abstract: This article presents a short summary of The Blind Spot: Why Science Cannot Ignore Human Experience by Adam Frank, Marcelo Gleiser, and Evan Thompson (Frank et al., 2024). We argue that the inability to see that lived experience is the ineliminable source of scientific knowledge and practice is a blind spot in our present scientific culture. We diagnose the philosophical and historical causes of the blind spot, and chart its manifestations across cosmology, quantum physics, biology, cognitive science, the neuroscience of consciousness, and Earth system science. This précis describes the book’s main philosophical ideas.

items.title: The Manuscript Dissemination of Descartes’s Traité de l’homme: With an Edition of the Tractatus de homine a Cartesio.
items.abstract: This book offers the first thorough-going account of the covert manuscript dissemination of a pivotal text in the history of early modern philosophy and science, namely the Traité de l’homme by René Descartes, completed in 1633 but published in printed form only in 1662 and 1664. This account serves as both introduction to and commentary upon the following transcription of a Latin handwritten translation of the treatise (Tractatus de homine a Cartesio) recently brought to the attention of scholars, and which was integral to such dissemination. Included is an apparatus of variants with respect to its first editions. Importantly, during its first dissemination the treatise fostered the development of medical theories based on mechanical ideas and is now increasingly at the centre of the attention of historians, thanks to the renewed appreciation of Descartes as a scientist rather than as a metaphysician. By developing an investigation taking into account not only professors and scientists, but also the importance of women, courtiers, publishers, soldiers, and the covert circulation of knowledge in the early modern age, this book contributes to the knowledge of scholars, students, and anybody interested in the early modern history of philosophy, science, intellectual history, and the history of the book in a crucial phase of the development of western thought.

items.title: Introduction.
items.pub: In The Manuscript Dissemination of Descartes’s Traité de l’homme: With an Edition of the Tractatus de homine a Cartesio. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 1-46.
items.venue: The Manuscript Dissemination of Descartes’s Traité de l’homme: With an Edition of the Tractatus de homine a Cartesio
items.abstract: In this chapter I provide a hypothetical reconstruction of the dissemination of the handwritten copies of René[aut]Descartes, René Descartes’s Traité de l’homme up to the appearance of its first printed editions in 1662 (Latin) and 1664 (French). I discuss the manuscripts copied by Antonie Studler van Surck, Alphonse Pollot[aut]Pollot, Alphonse, and Elisabeth of Bohemia[aut]Elisabeth of Bohemia, its dissemination through the Socinian circles (including Henricus Regius’s access to it), and among the Leiden Cartesians (Adriaan Heereboord[aut]Heereboord, Adriaan, Johannes[aut]De Raey, Johannesde Raey[aut]De Raey, Elisabeth, and Aernout Huyberts[aut]Huyberts, Aernout). Moreover, I relate the manuscripts to the various attempts at securing and publishing manuscripts of L’homme (by the Elzeviers, Pierre-Hector Chanut, and Claude[aut]Clerselier, Claude Clerselier). On the ground of this reconstruction I provide a discussion of the handwritten translation of the treatise recently brought to the attention of scholars (ms. ATH 1444Leiden, Universiteitsbibliotheekms. ATH 1444), relating it to the efforts at making sense of the text by the Leiden Cartesians, and showing that it conveys a version of the treatise akin to the one published (1662) by Florentius[aut]Schuyl, Florentius Schuyl (with which it agrees in a number of substantial readings), while Clerselier might have published a text revised by Descartes around 1647.

items.title: Edition of ATH 1444.
items.pub: In The Manuscript Dissemination of Descartes’s Traité de l’homme: With an Edition of the Tractatus de homine a Cartesio. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 47-110.
items.venue: The Manuscript Dissemination of Descartes’s Traité de l’homme: With an Edition of the Tractatus de homine a Cartesio
items.abstract: In this chapter I provide an edition, with an apparatus of different readings and comments, of the partial text of René Descartes’s Traité de l’homme conveyed in a Latin translation by the manuscript ATH 1444, now extant at the Bibliotheca Thysiana at Leiden (part of the Leiden Universiteitsbibliotheek), and titled Tractatus de homine a Cartesio. The readings are considered with respect to the Latin and French editions published by Florentius Schuyl (1662 and 1664) and Claude Clerselier (1664 and 1677). This transcription offers an overview of the differences between the foremost known versions of the treatise, tracing to (possible) author’s and editors’ interventions, with particular attention to those concerning conceptually loaded terms, errors in translation or transcription, references to (now) missing figures, and stylistic choices.

items.title: Can the Searlean Notion of Collective Intentionality and Power lead to Coercion?
items.abstract: John Searle argues for a notion of ‘collective intentionality’ that produces social actions with the attributed deontic status function on an external reason, simultaneously recognized by all the members. Social actions depend on the acceptance of a propositional attitude in the light of a constitutive rule and the ‘we intention’ of each member. However, Searle’s intentional theory of actions argues that human beings are rational in nature and freely choose to act as per a desire independent of reason; hence, offering a possibility of unreflective obedience towards social rules. What implications and considerations may emerge while explicating relationships between intentionality, intentional action, the notion of power, and coerced life? This paper assesses the scope of such collective participation (in the Searlean sense) that boils down to a coerced life. The viewpoint of a coerced life is examined along with the notion of intentionality and background, and how these notions translate into a concept of power.

items.title: The Group Agent Account and the Pluralistic Ignorance Problem.
items.abstract: In this article, I present a potential counterexample to Lackey’s Group Agent Account (GAA) of group beliefs. I argue that cases of pluralistic ignorance pose a problem for Lackey’s GAA because, in such cases, it systematically yields the wrong ascriptions of belief. I then discuss two ways to improve GAA, which I call GAA* and GAA**, that make it immune to the pluralistic ignorance problem. However, I argue that GAA* and GAA** face their own problems that cannot be straightforwardly solved without overfitting the account. I conclude by arguing that pluralistic ignorance is not a minor problem but one that generally affects summative approaches, such as GAA, and provides evidence in support of nonsummative accounts of group beliefs.

items.title: Explanatory reasons, actions, and the right fit.
items.abstract: Action explanations are answers given to questions of the form: “Why did A φ?” Explanatory reasons are the explanantia of such explanations. In the last 25 years, various accounts on the nature of explanatory reasons have been presented. Ac- cording to factivism, for instance, explanatory reasons are the facts that the agent believed and acted on. According to psychologism, in turn, explanatory reasons are the agent’s beliefs themselves. The primary goal of this paper is to show that there are cases in which an action explanation is required but that none of the pre- dominant accounts can deal with. A secondary goal is to show that the predominant accounts have also misunderstood the exact purpose of action explanations. Action explanations – given as answers to questions of the form “Why did A φ?” – are not supposed to explain actions simpliciter. They are supposed to explain actions under a description that the questioner chose.

items.title: Naturalizing Phenomenal Intentionality.
items.pub: In Alberto Voltolini, Marking the Mark of the Mental. Springer Cham. pp. 77-102.
items.venue: Marking the Mark of the Mental
items.abstract: According to the phenomenal intentionality theory (PIT), intentionality is grounded in phenomenal consciousness: the qualitative and subjective character of experience, which makes possible the intentionality of mental states.
